title: The round city
hook: the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur founds Baghdad as a round city on the Tigris

segments.voice: Yesterday, al-Dakhil, the one who escaped: Abd al-Rahman swam the Euphrates and built a new state in al-Andalus. Your line was: he started again. What first step did you take? Day nine hundred thirteen. A new part begins: the Abbasids.

Night, on the bank of the Tigris. Workers have marked out the plan of a city on the bare ground with lines of ash. Now, al-Tabari reports, the caliph orders the lines laid over with cotton seeds soaked in naphtha, and set alight. The whole plan of the city flares up in fire on the dark earth, so the caliph can walk it and see it whole before a single brick is laid. And the shape burning in the dark is a circle. The caliph is al-Mansur, of the new Abbasid house, and the city is Baghdad. Today: the round city.
screen: `LINES OF ASH ON THE GROUND.` → `SET ALIGHT AT NIGHT.` → `A CIRCLE OF FIRE.`

segments.voice: Why a new city? The Abbasids had overthrown a dynasty based in Damascus, and their strength lay east, in Iraq and Khurasan. Al-Mansur wanted a capital of his own. He chose a spot on the Tigris, where boats and roads could bring the trade of many lands. He gave it an official name: Madinat al-Salam, the City of Peace. Some readers hear in it an echo of the Qur'an, where God is said to call people to the abode of peace. Then the shape. The old descriptions tell of a city ringed by walls, with gates opening onto the great roads, each named for where its road led: the Kufa gate, the Basra gate, the Khurasan gate, the Syria gate. At the very center stood the caliph's palace, crowned by a green dome, with the great mosque beside it. The walls ran all the way around it. Consider what that says. The ruler sits at the center, and the great roads of the empire run to his door. It's a city drawn as a picture of power. Yet the circle didn't hold. Markets and neighborhoods spilled out past the walls almost from the start, and Baghdad grew in every direction, across the river and beyond. The round city itself is long gone. We know it now only from the descriptions of writers who saw it or heard about it. A perfect circle, drawn in fire, and then the life of a real city overflowing it.
screen: `A CAPITAL OF THEIR OWN.` · `THE CITY OF PEACE.` · `GATES TO THE FOUR ROADS.` · then, large: `THE PALACE AT THE CENTER.`

segments.voice: The practice: draw a circle. If you have paper and a pen, draw one now, as round as you can. It won't be perfect. That's fine. Put a dot at the center. Sit with it, and breathe. Ask: what sits at the center of my days right now? Work, worry, a person, a phone? Breathe in. Then ask: what would I want there instead? Breathe out. If you like, write that word in the center of your circle. If you pray, you can bring to mind the name the city was given, the City of Peace, and ask for peace in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Al-Mansur, the Abbasid caliph who had Baghdad's plan burned into the dark earth in lines of fire, and raised his round city on the Tigris around it. Today's word.
Your line: a circle, drawn in fire. Today, keep your circle somewhere you'll see it, and notice what pulls at the center of your day. Day nine hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: Historians reconstruct the round city of Baghdad from written descriptions by al-Tabari, al-Ya'qubi and al-Khatib al-Baghdadi, since little or nothing of it can be seen today.
